positions/original-sin-as-sickness/oneLi: What we inherit from Adam is a disease or bent toward self-love, not personal guilt; it inevitably leads to actual sin and needs healing in Christ, but infants of believers are not damned for it.
positions/original-sin-as-sickness/coreC: Sin in the proper sense requires transgression of a law; original sin is a condition or defect.
The inherited condition is real, universal and deadly.
Children of Christian parents dying in infancy are saved through the covenant.
positions/original-sin-as-sickness/origi: Articulated by Huldrych Zwingli in his Declaration on Original Sin (1526); related to later Arminian (Remonstrant) and Wesleyan accounts of inherited depravity without inherited guilt, and to some Baptist and Anabaptist teaching on the innocence of infants.
positions/original-sin-as-sickness/stron: It affirms sin’s universality and depth without imputing personal guilt to infants.
It respects Ezekiel 18’s principle that children do not bear the guilt of parents.
It provides pastoral comfort concerning infants who die.
Lutheran and Reformed confessions criticised it as minimising sin (Augsburg Confession II condemns those who deny original vice is truly sin).
Augustinians argue that Romans 5 speaks of condemnation, not merely disease.
Some critics see it as a step toward Pelagianism.
positions/original-sin-as-sickness/respo: Zwinglians answer that a deadly disease inevitably producing sin is hardly minimal.
They argue that Romans 5:13 itself distinguishes sin “not imputed where there is no law”.
positions/original-sin-as-sickness/conse: Shaped Anabaptist and Baptist views of the age of accountability.
Anticipated later Arminian and Wesleyan anthropology.
positions/total-depravity/name: Total depravity and the bound will
positions/total-depravity/oneLine: Sin has corrupted every part of fallen human nature — mind, will, affections and body — so that, apart from regenerating grace, no one can or will turn to God; humans remain free from coercion but are bound in their will.
positions/total-depravity/coreClaims/0: Depravity is “total” in extent (affecting every faculty), not that humans are as evil as possible.
positions/total-depravity/coreClaims/1: The unregenerate will is in bondage to sin and cannot choose God.
positions/total-depravity/coreClaims/3: Civil goodness remains by common grace, but no work can merit salvation.
positions/total-depravity/origin: Based on Augustine’s late anti-Pelagian writings; sharpened by Luther’s The Bondage of the Will (1525) against Erasmus and by Calvin; confessed at Dort (1619, third and fourth heads) and Westminster (ch. 9).
positions/total-depravity/strongestArgum: It takes seriously the Bible’s language of spiritual death, not mere illness.
It magnifies grace: salvation is wholly God’s work.
It matches the experience of conversion as rescue rather than self-improvement.
positions/total-depravity/strongestObjec: Arminians and Wesleyans object that it makes divine commands and invitations insincere if humans cannot respond.
Catholics and Orthodox argue that the image of God and free will, though wounded, remain.
Critics argue it can foster fatalism or a low view of human goodness.
positions/total-depravity/responses/0: Reformed theologians answer that inability is moral, not natural: humans cannot because they will not.
positions/total-depravity/responses/1: They hold that God uses commands and invitations as the very means by which he regenerates.
positions/total-depravity/consequences/0: Central to Lutheran and Reformed soteriology and the TULIP scheme.
positions/total-depravity/consequences/1: Shaped revivalist preaching of the need for new birth.
positions/prevenient-grace/oneLine: Humans are totally unable by nature to turn to God, but God gives to all people a “preventing” (going-before) grace that restores enough freedom to respond to the gospel, so that salvation is wholly by grace yet resistible.
positions/prevenient-grace/coreClaims/0: Original sin leaves humanity dead in sin and unable to seek God by nature.
positions/prevenient-grace/coreClaims/1: Through Christ’s atonement God gives prevenient grace to every person.
positions/prevenient-grace/coreClaims/2: This grace enables but does not compel faith; it can be resisted.
positions/prevenient-grace/coreClaims/3: Conscience and longings for God in all people are signs of this grace.
positions/prevenient-grace/origin: Grounded in patristic and medieval teaching on grace preceding the will (Orange 529 spoke of prevenient grace); developed by Jacobus Arminius and the Remonstrance (1610); central to John Wesley’s theology and to Methodist, Holiness and Pentecostal traditions.
positions/prevenient-grace/strongestArgu: It holds together human depravity, the universal love of God and genuine human responsibility.
It explains the universal sense of conscience and longing for God.
It makes God’s universal invitations sincere.
positions/prevenient-grace/strongestObje: Calvinists object that the doctrine has thin explicit biblical support and makes the decisive difference in salvation a human choice.
Lutherans note it may reintroduce synergism.
Some argue that a universal grace that restores free will is, in effect, a denial of total depravity.
positions/prevenient-grace/responses/0: Wesleyans answer that John 1:9 and 12:32 imply a universal enlightening and drawing.
positions/prevenient-grace/responses/1: They insist that the ability to respond is itself grace, so no one can boast.
positions/prevenient-grace/consequences/: Foundational for Methodist evangelism and global Holiness-Pentecostal movements.
Shaped hymnody (“Thy sovereign grace to all extends”).
positions/libertarian-freedom/oneLine: A free choice is one not determined by prior causes, including God’s decree; the agent could have chosen otherwise in the same circumstances, and only such freedom grounds moral responsibility.
positions/libertarian-freedom/coreClaims: Responsibility requires the ability to do otherwise.
God gave creatures genuine freedom, which he respects.
Divine foreknowledge (or middle knowledge, or an open future) does not cause choices.
Sin originates in a free creaturely choice, not in God’s will.
positions/libertarian-freedom/origin: Assumed by most early Fathers (Justin, Irenaeus, Origen, Gregory of Nyssa, Chrysostom) against fatalism; defended by Erasmus (1524), Molina (1588) and Arminius; elaborated in modern analytic philosophy (Plantinga, Swinburne, Kane).
positions/libertarian-freedom/strongestA: It best explains moral responsibility and divine commands.
It distances God from authorship of sin.
It reflects the near-unanimous view of the pre-Augustinian Fathers.
positions/libertarian-freedom/strongestO: Compatibilists argue that undetermined choices are random rather than free, and the agent’s character becomes irrelevant.
Calvinists argue it limits God’s sovereignty and contradicts texts where God determines human choices (Proverbs 21:1).
Some ask how God can infallibly foreknow undetermined choices.
positions/libertarian-freedom/responses/: Libertarians propose agent-causation or “self-forming actions” (Kane) to answer the randomness objection.
They appeal to middle knowledge or eternity to reconcile freedom with foreknowledge.
positions/libertarian-freedom/consequenc: Underpins free-will theodicy, Molinism, Arminianism and open theism.
Central to Eastern synergy and theosis.
positions/compatibilist-freedom/oneLine: Human freedom means acting according to one’s own desires and reasons without external coercion; such freedom is compatible with the will being determined by one’s nature, motives and ultimately God’s decree.
positions/compatibilist-freedom/coreClai: We are free when we do what we want; we are not free to want otherwise than our nature inclines.
The will follows the strongest motive or greatest apparent good.
God can ordain all things without coercing creatures, so responsibility remains.
Fallen humans freely sin; regenerated humans freely love God.
positions/compatibilist-freedom/origin: Anticipated by Augustine (freedom as delight in the good) and Luther; given classic form by Jonathan Edwards (Freedom of the Will, 1754); held in Reformed theology and by many analytic philosophers.
positions/compatibilist-freedom/stronges: It explains how God can sovereignly ordain all events while humans remain responsible.
It gives an intelligible account of choices as flowing from character.
It explains the freedom of the saints in heaven, who cannot sin yet are truly free.
Libertarians object that if choices are determined, agents could not have done otherwise and so cannot be blamed.
It appears to make God the ultimate cause of sin.
Critics argue it redefines freedom so that it no longer means what ordinary people mean.
positions/compatibilist-freedom/response: Compatibilists answer that responsibility attaches to acting from one’s own will, as Frankfurt-style cases suggest.
They distinguish God’s ordaining from his approving and stress secondary causation.
positions/compatibilist-freedom/conseque: Central to Reformed providence and soteriology.
positions/federal-forensic-framework/one: God the righteous Judge has bound humanity to himself by covenant; Adam’s sin brought guilt and condemnation on all he represented, and Christ, the second federal head, fulfilled the law and bore its penalty for his people, whose sins are forgiven and to whom his righteousness is imputed through faith.
positions/federal-forensic-framework/cor: God relates to humanity through covenants: a covenant of works with Adam and a covenant of grace in Christ (Westminster Confession 7).
Sin is primarily guilt and liability to punishment before God’s holy law; Adam’s guilt is imputed to his posterity.
Christ’s active obedience and passive suffering satisfy divine justice as substitute for the elect (penal substitution).
Justification is a forensic verdict: sins pardoned and Christ’s righteousness imputed, received by faith alone; sanctification follows as a distinct work.
Union with Christ is affirmed, often as the federal and mystical bond through which justification is applied.
positions/federal-forensic-framework/ori: Developed from Reformation forensic justification (Melanchthon, Calvin) into federal theology (Ursinus, Olevianus, Cocceius), codified in the Westminster Standards (1646-47); expounded by John Owen, Francis Turretin, Charles Hodge and the Princeton theology; restated by J. I. Packer, R. C. Sproul and John Piper.
positions/federal-forensic-framework/str: It explains Paul’s courtroom vocabulary (justify, condemn, reckon, impute) on its own terms.
It grounds assurance outside the believer, in Christ’s finished obedience and a once-for-all verdict.
It preserves the seriousness of sin, the holiness of God and the necessity of personal faith and repentance.
Union critics (Campbell, the Torrances): it makes God’s relation to humanity fundamentally legal rather than filial, and turns covenant into contract.
Orthodox: it reduces salvation to a change of status, neglecting healing and theosis.
New Perspective: it reads Paul through late-medieval and Reformation anxieties about merit.
positions/federal-forensic-framework/res: Federal theologians reply that the law expresses God’s own holy character and that adoption and union are inseparable from justification.
Recent Reformed scholarship (Fesko, Gaffin) stresses that union with Christ has always been the context of forensic justification in Reformed theology.
positions/federal-forensic-framework/con: Shaped Puritan and Presbyterian piety, revival preaching and much of modern evangelicalism.
Encourages careful distinction of justification and sanctification, law and gospel.
